document.title: European Institutions vs FOSS communities
document.subtitle: A comparative reading of software development and security practices
document.purpose: Expose where European Institutions and FOSS communities differ in development and security practice, and where each side has lessons for the other.
document.core_question: Which software-development and security practices are stronger in institutional projects, which are stronger in FOSS communities, and what should each improve?

editorial_policy.notes: The 46-page deliverable is reorganized around the report's ten comparison areas and its own executive conclusions.

design_system.notes: Institutional blue retained with red accent; page-by-page deliverable structure is compressed.

evidence.text: The study compares software development methodologies used in European Institutions and FOSS communities, with conclusions for the future evolution of development methodologies in European Institutions.

The comparison is organised across ten areas, including project management, software development methodology, security definition, testing, release management, code review, authentication and authorisation, incident management, problem management and licensing.
European Institutions manage project management activities more efficiently than FOSS communities; FOSS communities should improve this area according to their resources.
For software security definition, both European Institutions and FOSS communities should improve; the report states that security awareness in FOSS communities is higher.
European Institutions have resources for software security testing but do not perform it regularly or for all projects; FOSS communities should improve security knowledge and testing frequency.
FOSS communities are efficient in inspection and code review but should add security code review; European Institutions should involve security experts and promote security awareness.
The report says FOSS communities are better at incident management; European Institutions should improve user notification and critical-incident processes.
The report says FOSS communities are more efficient at problem management, while recommending improvements for both sides.
For each comparison area, the study summarises evidence, compares factors such as workforce, documentation, processes, resources, tools and benefits, then derives conclusions and recommendations.

scenes.message: Institutional discipline and open-source practice are compared area by area.
scenes.title: Not one model against another. Ten practices under comparison.
scenes.body: The deliverable asks where European Institutions and FOSS communities differ in development and security practice, then turns those differences into recommendations.

transformations.description: The deliverable's purpose and ten-area scope are elevated before the detailed sections.

scenes.message: The report follows a repeatable compare-and-recommend logic.
scenes.title: Evidence → comparison → recommendation.

steps.title: Summarise the evidence
steps.headline: Start with observed practice
steps.text: For each area, the study consolidates material from previous deliverables.

steps.title: Compare the factors
steps.headline: Use the same lenses
steps.text: Workforce, documentation, processes, resources, tools and benefits structure the comparison.

steps.title: Derive actions
steps.headline: Turn differences into recommendations
steps.text: The study concludes each area with recommendations linked to the observed strengths and weaknesses.

transformations.description: The methodological paragraph is converted into a three-step sequence.

scenes.message: Formal resources and process maturity favour European Institutions in some areas, but do not guarantee security practice is consistently applied.
scenes.title: More structure does not automatically mean more security practice.

items.title: Institutional advantage
items.text: The report judges European Institutions more efficient and mature in project-management practice.

items.title: Resources exist, regularity does not
items.text: Institutions can perform many forms of testing, but the report says it is not done regularly or across all projects.

transformations.description: Two executive-summary conclusions are placed together to distinguish process capacity from consistent security execution.

scenes.message: The report gives FOSS communities stronger marks in several operational practices while still identifying security gaps.
scenes.title: Openness creates different strengths.

items.title: Security definition
items.text: The report says FOSS security awareness is higher, while recommending improvements to both sides.

items.title: Inspection & code review
items.text: FOSS communities are described as efficient in code review, but should add explicit security review.

items.title: Incident management
items.text: FOSS communities are assessed as better at managing incidents.

items.title: Problem management
items.text: FOSS communities are assessed as more efficient at tackling problems, partly because their open nature exposes them to problems more frequently.

transformations.description: Four source conclusions are assembled as a bounded set of FOSS strengths and remaining gaps.

scenes.message: Neither operating model owns every good practice.
scenes.body: Institutional projects bring formal process and resources. FOSS communities bring strong review, incident and problem-solving habits. The report's recommendations run in both directions.

transformations.description: The report's area-by-area conclusions are synthesised into the reciprocal learning pattern they collectively support.

scenes.message: Security improvement comes from combining formal governance with the practices that openness makes routine.
scenes.title: Borrow the strengths. Keep the evidence.

transformations.description: The close condenses the study's reciprocal recommendations without inventing a single preferred methodology.
